title: Lesson 16: Worked Example A: An Ops and Reporting Workflow, End to End
description: Worked example A: an ops and reporting workflow, end to end. What a worked example, an ops workflow, and a reporting workflow are, why a single source of truth and a review gate matter, and how the reliability pieces catch a real failure in a recurring report.

questions.question: Nadia's weekly operations report came back with an impossible 99.4 percent on-time rate. She checked her changelog and found the tracker had added a new status field that the pull step was reading as blank, and the compute step was counting blank as on time. Per the lesson, what is the right diagnosis and fix?
options: The fault is at the handoff between the tracker and the pull step, so she should map the new status code to the on-time flag before the compute step reads it, then log the change
The fault is inside the compute prompt, so she should rewrite the whole compute step from scratch without touching the pull step
The fault is in the report output, so she should change where the report is posted before examining the steps
The fault is unfixable, so she should abandon the workflow and build the report by hand every week
questions.explanation: The lesson's failure story is exactly this: the tracker changed what it exports, the pull step expected the old on-time flag, and the compute step inherited the flaw. The changelog let Nadia find the change in minutes, and the fix was one line mapping the new status code to the on-time flag before the compute step reads it. This is the garbage-in, garbage-out principle made concrete: the input changed shape and the whole report inherited it. Rewriting the compute step, blaming the output, or reverting to manual work all skip the diagnosis the lesson teaches.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does a reporting workflow need a single source of truth?
options: Because if two reports count the same metric differently, the reports disagree, and the disagreement is worse than either wrong number since nobody knows which to trust
Because a report is only useful if it is formatted as a polished document for a reader
Because a single source of truth only matters at the very end of the flow, never in the middle
Because keeping your own copy of the numbers makes the report faster to produce each week
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a single source of truth as the one agreed place a number comes from, and explains that if two reports count the same metric differently, the reports disagree, and the disagreement is worse than either wrong number because nobody knows which to trust. Nadia pulls from the tracker and incident log rather than keeping her own copy, so the report never disagrees with the real system. The other options contradict the core idea.

questions.question: Nadia's workflow has six steps: trigger, data pull, compute, draft, review gate, and output. Per the lesson, why does the review gate earn a pause while the data pull does not?
options: Because the report is externally visible and expensive to get wrong, so a human belongs in that loop, while the pull is routine and reversible and earns rhythm, not a pause
Because the data pull is the hardest step and needs a human to check every number
Because the review gate is the only step that produces any output at all
Because the trigger should always be the step that stops for human approval
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the review-gate test from Lesson 13: a step earns a pause when a miss costs too much. The report to leadership is externally visible and a wrong number in it is expensive to unwind, so it earns a gate. The data pull is routine and reversible, so it earns rhythm, not a pause. This is what keeps the workflow fast where it can be and careful where it must be. The other options reverse the reasoning.
